25   The chosen AD conditions mimic the operational conditions of the AnMBR. The effluent flow of

26    the AD (which is similar to the permeate flow of the AnMBR), was set as influent flow to the DAF

27   system (Qp). Thus, based on the design parameters shown in Tables A.1 and A.2, the lab-scale

28  DAF had a volume of 0.19 L, a height of around 10 cm, and a diameter od around 5 cm. The final

29  DAF influent entitles the before mentioned effluent flow plus the recirculation flow, as shown in

30   Figure A.

33   To calculate the oxygen load in the DAF system the following assumptions were made:

34         -  No oxygen escapes the system (Qgas0). This would be the worse case scenario in which

35           the anaerobic biomass in the AD would be subjected to the highest amount of oxygen.

36         -   Air is assumed to be composed of 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen.

37         -   Dissolution of air at the gicen pressure (or air transfer efficiency) is assumed to be at 70%

38            in accordance to Wang, et al. [2].

39         -   Dissolved oxygen and nitrogen were calculated based on Henry’s constants for oxygen and

40           nitrogen (1.2 ×10-3 and 6.5 ×10-4, respectively) and correcting for the desire temperature

41             [3].

43   comparison to the AD COD inflow.

278  SUPPORTING INFORMATION E
279   To further understand the reasons behind the high methane concentration in the biogas, the effect

280    of pH in the dissolved concentrations of total inorganic carbon produced (TIC), HCO3-, CO2, and

281    CO32-, was assessed in the PhreeqC model. The total dissolved carbon concentration from these

282    three species increased by around 3% in the MA-AnMBR compared to the AnMBR period. At a

283  pH of 7.6, the MA-AnMBR had a dissolved carbon concentration of 0.42 g∙L-1, while at a pH of

284    7.4 it was 0.41 g∙L-1 for the AnMBR. The most significant change was observed for carbonic

285    acid, where the model predicted an HCO3-1 concentration of 2.03 g∙L-1 for the MA-AnMBR state

286   and 1.92 g∙L-1 for the AnMBR. Moreover, dissolved CO2 concentration was also assessed at a

287    neutral pH, and results showed that for both periods, the dissolved CO2 concentration was

288   0.35 g∙L-1. This value could also be linked to the predicted increase of CO2 concentration in the

289   biogas at pH 7, which was around 14 % for both reactor states.


290   Aside from an increase in the total inorganic carbon produced, the high acid neutralization

291    capacity (ANC) of the AnMBR and MA-AnMBR could be linked to the urea concentration of

292    the feed. A concentration of 1.0 g∙L-1 of urea was added to the synthetic feed. Urea has a molar

293   mass of 60 g.mol-1, and each mmol of urea is responsible for producing two meq of ammonia

294   and one of carbon dioxide. At the lab-scale reactor pH, ammonia and carbon dioxide will be

295   mainly in the form of NH4+ and HCO3-, obtaining a surplus of 17 meq of NH4+ cations. Most of

296    the feed’s COD content comes from sodium acetate and cellulose, added in concentrations of 2.6

297   and 1.5 g∙L-1. The first one uses its own sodium as a buffer, and most of the sodium acetate is

298   converted to methane and NaHCO3 [4]. The produced CO2 from cellulose will be chemically

299   bound with the surplus of NH4+ cations coming from urea. This will decrease the CO2 content in

300    biogas, (increasing the partial content of CH4), and improve the system buffer capacity, raising

301    the ANC/TIC ratio. A rise in this ratio increases the HCO3- concentration in the liquid and

302    decreases the biogas CO2 concentration [5]. Therefore, the high methane concentration of the

303   biogas for the AnMBR and MA-AnMBR could be attributed to the feed characteristics, high urea

304    concentration, and CO2 dissolution into the liquid.


305    Results of the PhreeqC model regarding methane and carbon dioxide biogas concentrations were

306    further tested with the influent and reactor conditions given by Ozgun, et al. [6], which uses urea

307    as one of the main sources of ammonium. For the lab-scale reactor operated at a pH of 7, Ozgun,

308    et al. obtained a CH4 concentration of 61 ± 5.7%, while the model predicted a methane

309    concentration of 61%. Moreover, for the same conditions, at a pH of 7.65, the results of the

310   model showed an expected biogas methane concentration of 88%.

338  SUPPORTING INFORMATION G
339   Methods for microbial community analysis

340              DNA extraction
341          Three triplicate sludge samples were taken to perform microbial population analysis, one

342   from the AnMBR state (after 150 days of operation), and two from the MA-AnMBR state (after

343   370 and 580 days of operation). A homogenised sludge sample of 1.5 mL was transferred into an

344   Eppendorf tube and centrifuged in a micro-centrifuge (Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany), to extract

345  DNA. Around 50 mg of sludge pellet were added to the extraction tubes from the soil FastDNA

346    spin kit (MP Biomedicals, Irvine, CA, U.S.). DNA extraction was performed following the

347    protocol established by Albertsen, et al. [7]. The concentration of the extracted DNA was measured

348   using a Qubit dsDNA assay kit (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, U.S.A). Finally, the DNA samples

349   were frozen at -25 °C until they were sent for gene amplification.

350               16S rRNA Gene Amplicon Sequencing and Data Analysis
351         The 16sRNA gene was selected for amplification and paired-end sequence, in an Ilumina

352   NovaSeq 6000 platform by Novogene (Beijing, China). The primer set chosen to amplify and

353   sequence the hypervariable region V3-V4 was 341F [50’CCTAYGGGRBGCASCAG–3’] and

354   806R [5’–GGACTACNNGGGTATCTAAT–3’].  Subsequently,  the Sequence Read Archive

355   (SRA) of the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) was used for reading the raw

356    data. The gene sequence provided by Novogene was further processed and analysed following the

357   procedure developed by[8] Amir, et al. [8], Toja Ortega, et al. [9].

358   Results and discussion

359        To obtain insight in the micro-organisms specific response to the induced oxygen stress

360  DNA analysis was performed for the three samples, the AnMBR state (after 150 days of operation),

361   and two from the MA-AnMBR state (after 370 and 580 days of operation). The two most relatively

362   abundant taxa for the MA-AnMBR samples were bacteria family Thermofonsia or SBR103 and

363    archaeal family Methanosaetaceae, while these taxa were the second and fifth most abundant in

364    the AnMBR samples, respectively. Alpha and beta diversity analyses were conducted to identify

365    further differences between the two reactor states. The diversity within samples (alpha diversity)

366   showed that the phylogenetic distance between taxa in each sample was statistically different (p-

367   value of 0.03), whilst the community evenness within samples was insignificant. Even though the

368    diversity analysis showed a statistical difference between the AnMBR and MA-AnMBR sludge

369   samples, it cannot be linked to differences in AD performance [10].

370         However, the sequencing of the 16rRNA is not useful to define microorganisms that are

371    responsible for specific processes [11]. For instance, whilst Methanosaetaceae family relative

372   abundance increased from 6.2 to 20.7% from the AnMBR to the MA-AnMBR samples (taken after

373   150 and 370 days respectively), no statistical difference was observed in this group due to the low

374    relative abundance of Methanosaetaceae in the Archaea kingdom. While most hydrogenotrophic

375   methanogens are members of the family of Methanobacteriaceae [12], aceticlastic methanogens

376   belong to the family of Methanosaetaceae [4]. No changes were observed between the sludge

377   samples from the AnMBR and MA-AnMBR in the relative abundance of both families in the

378   Archaea kingdom. Methanobacteriaceae represented around 3.5% of the Archaea while the

379    aceticlastic methanogens were around 95.5%. Since hydrogenotrophic and aceticlastic bacteria’s

380    relative abundance between the reactor periods did not vary, and SMA results showed no statistical

381   changes in the MA-AnMBR sludge subjected to small aeration, changes in biogas production were

382    not expected.
